html:
The Indo-Greek kingdoms were states in Gandhara and Punjab ruled by Greek kings for about two centuries, from about 180 BCE to about 10 CE. They were the far eastern end of the world that Alexander had opened.

They began when Demetrius I, Greek king of Bactria, crossed the Hindu Kush as the Maurya Empire fell apart. More than thirty kings followed, known mostly from their coins. The coins carry fine Greek portraits on one side and Indian scripts and symbols on the other.

The best known king is Menander, who ruled from Sagala, today's Sialkot, about 150 BCE. He appears in the Buddhist book Milinda Panha, "Questions of Milinda", where he debates with the monk Nagasena and becomes a Buddhist. A Greek envoy, Heliodorus, set up a pillar to Vishnu at Vidisha that still stands.

Shaka and then Kushan invaders took the kingdoms over. What lasted was the mix: Greek sculpture put to Buddhist use became the art of Gandhara, and Indian astronomy took the zodiac and other ideas from Greek books.
sum: The Indo-Greek kingdoms were states in Gandhara and Punjab ruled by Greek kings for about two centuries, from about 180 BCE to about 10 CE. They were the far eastern end of the world that Alexander had opened.
